# Rolling {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Smoothing without losing the axis

`resample` gives you fewer, coarser points. A **rolling window** keeps every
point and averages each with its neighbours.

```python
q.rolling(window=30, center=True).mean()
```

::: {.fragment}
Use resample when you want monthly *values*. Use rolling when you want to see
the shape of a season on a daily axis.
:::

## `center=True` costs you the ends

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 10
import pandas as pd, numpy as np

idx = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=400, freq="D")
q = pd.Series(np.abs(np.sin(np.arange(400) / 58)) * 40, index=idx)

for w in [7, 30, 365]:
    r = q.rolling(w, center=True).mean()
    print(f"window {w:4d}: {r.notna().sum():4d} values, {r.isna().sum():3d} lost at the ends")
```

::: {.fragment}
A centred 365-day mean cannot be computed for the first or last 182 days — half
the window falls outside the data. That is honest.
:::

## The alternative is worse

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`center=True`**

Each average is labelled with the middle of its window.

Costs half a window at each end.

*Use when describing data.*
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**`center=False`** (default)

Each average is labelled with the **last** day of its window.

Shifts every feature later by half a window.

*Use when simulating something that could only know the past.*
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
The default is `False`. If you are plotting a smoothed history and you don't set
`center=True`, your peaks are in the wrong place by half a window — and nothing
warns you.
:::

## Your turn: the wettest sustained month

A single-day peak is a flood. A high 30-day average is a wet season, and water
managers care about the second one.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_roll
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
idx = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=400, freq="D")
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
q = pd.Series(np.abs(np.sin(np.arange(400) / 58)) * 40 + rng.gamma(1, 3, 400), index=idx)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_roll
rolling_30 = q.rolling(______, center=True).mean()
wettest = ______
print(f"wettest 30-day mean: {rolling_30.max():.1f}, centred on {wettest:%Y-%m-%d}")
print(f"single wettest day:  {q.max():.1f}")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_roll"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`.idxmax()` gives the *index label* at the maximum — here, a date. `.max()`
gives the value.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_roll"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
rolling_30 = q.rolling(30, center=True).mean()
wettest = rolling_30.idxmax()
```

In the real Sabino record the peak day is about ten times the wettest sustained
month. That gap is the whole difference between flood hydrology and
water-supply hydrology, and it is why the two fields argue about which statistic
matters.
:::
:::

# Grouping {background-color="#AB0520"}

## The key can be anything

```python
levels.groupby("site_no")                        # a column
levels.groupby(levels["date"].dt.year)           # something you computed
levels.groupby([(y // 10) * 10])                 # decades
levels.groupby(["site_no", "year"])              # two keys
```

::: {.fragment}
Split, apply, combine. The only interesting part is choosing the split.
:::

## `.agg()` gives several answers at once

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 11
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "site": ["A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B"],
    "depth": [31.0, 44.5, 52.1, 88.0, 91.2, 86.4],
})

print(df.groupby("site")["depth"].agg(
    n="size", first="first", last="last", deepest="max"
))
```

::: {.fragment}
One pass, four answers, and named columns. Three separate `groupby` calls would
read worse and cost three passes.
:::

## Your turn: how widespread is the decline?

Each well's change is `last - first`. Summarise across all of them.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_group
import pandas as pd
summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "change_ft": [46.8, -3.2, 111.0, 22.4, -8.1, 67.3, 5.0, 89.9],
}, index=["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H"])
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_group
n_declining = ______
n_recovering = ______
median_change = ______
print(f"{n_declining} declining, {n_recovering} recovering, median {median_change:+.1f} ft")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_group"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Depth counts downward, so a **positive** change means the water table fell.
Summing a boolean Series counts the `True`s.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_group"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
n_declining = (summary["change_ft"] > 0).sum()
n_recovering = (summary["change_ft"] < 0).sum()
median_change = summary["change_ft"].median()
```

6 declining, 2 recovering, median +34.6 ft.

In the real 80-well dataset it is **73 declining with a median of 46.8 ft**.
That is not a handful of overpumped wells; that is a basin.
:::
:::

# Long and wide {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Two shapes for the same data

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Long**

One row per measurement.

```
site   date        depth
A-14   2019-04-02   86.4
A-14   2020-03-18   88.1
B-07   2019-04-02   41.2
```

Compact. What analysis wants.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Wide**

One column per series.

```
date         A-14   B-07
2019-04-02   86.4   41.2
2020-03-18   88.1    NaN
```

Sparse. What plotting wants.
:::
:::

## `pivot_table` and `melt`

```python
wide = levels.pivot_table(index="date", columns="site_no",
                          values="depth_to_water_ft")

long = wide.reset_index().melt(id_vars="date", var_name="site_no",
                               value_name="depth_to_water_ft").dropna()
```

::: {.fragment}
For the real dataset: 9,046 measurements become a **4,731 × 80** table — 378,480
cells, **98% of them empty**, because no two wells were visited on the same days.
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
That is the trade. For irregular field data, stay long as long as you can.
:::

## Your turn: reshape and count

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_pivot
import pandas as pd
long = pd.DataFrame({
    "site_no": ["A", "A", "B", "B", "C"],
    "date": pd.to_datetime(["2019-01-01", "2020-01-01",
                            "2019-01-01", "2021-01-01", "2020-01-01"]),
    "depth_ft": [31.0, 33.5, 88.0, 91.2, 55.0],
})
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_pivot
wide = long.pivot_table(index=______, columns=______, values="depth_ft")
n_empty = ______
print(wide)
print(f"{n_empty} of {wide.size} cells are empty")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_pivot"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Dates down the side, wells across the top. `.isna().sum().sum()` counts missing
cells across the whole frame — two sums because the first gives one number per
column.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_pivot"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
wide = long.pivot_table(index="date", columns="site_no", values="depth_ft")
n_empty = wide.isna().sum().sum()
```

4 of 9 cells empty, from five measurements. Even at this size the sparsity is
obvious; at 80 wells it is 98%.

Note `pivot_table` silently **averages** duplicates, where `pivot` raises. That
is either a convenience or a way to hide a data problem, depending on whether
you checked for duplicates first — which is why we did that last week.
:::
:::

## Wrap up {.smaller}

::: {.kicker}
What you did today
:::

- `rolling(center=True)` costs half a window at each end and is worth it
- Group by anything, including a key you compute on the spot
- `.agg()` names its outputs and makes one pass
- Wide is convenient and sparse; long is compact and awkward
